steps.prompt: Where does a word like sometimes or often go?
options: Before the main verb, but after am / is / are
At the end of the sentence, always
steps.answer: Before the main verb, but after am / is / are
steps.why: He sometimes thinks (before the verb) but It is often (after be).

steps.title: Adverbs of frequency
steps.html:
AdverbPositionExample
alwaysbefore the main verbI always get up at six.
usuallybefore the main verbShe usually works at home.
oftenbefore the main verbWe often go to the gym.
sometimesbefore the verb, or firstSometimes I stay in.
rarelybefore the main verbHe rarely goes out.
neverbefore the main verbHe never does housework.
with beafter am / is / areI am never late.

One-word adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never) go before the main verb.

With am / is / are they go after the verb: She is always busy.

Expressions of frequency (every day, once a week, twice a month, three times a year) go at the end of the sentence: He goes to the gym twice a week.

Never is already negative. Say I never do housework, not I don’t never do housework.

Ask about frequency with the question form from Lesson 1: How often do you …?

steps.title: Before you read: a night nurse, a freelancer and a farmer.
steps.sub: Who do you think sleeps least? Choose one, then read and find out whether you were right.

steps.title: The average day — and three people who don’t have one
steps.html:
Every year the American government asks thousands of people one question: what did you do yesterday, hour by hour? The answers become the American Time Use Survey — an average day that almost nobody lives.

A full-time worker works 8.4 hours on a weekday and 5.6 hours at the weekend. Eighty per cent of employed people work on a weekday, but only thirty per cent work at the weekend. They sleep about nine hours and spend nearly five on leisure, half of it television.

That is the average. Here are three people nowhere near it.

Aliya is a night nurse. Her shift runs from seven in the evening to seven in the morning. She hardly ever eats a proper meal at work, and she rarely sleeps well: nurses sleep about eighty-three minutes less before a shift. On her days off she stays in, does the housework, helps her son with his homework and goes swimming twice a week.

Dias is a freelancer. A third of employed people now work from home; Dias does it every day. He writes a to-do list each morning and works indoors until dark. He often works late. He never goes to the gym and gave up running years ago, but he plays chess online twice a week.

Ruslan is a farmer. He gets up early, always, even in winter, and spends the day outdoors. His work is his exercise. In summer he hardly ever has a free weekend, but every October he goes camping.

The survey gives you a number. It does not give you a day. Ask any of the three of them what a normal week looks like, and all three will tell you theirs is completely ordinary.

Sources. All national figures: American Time Use Survey 2024, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — a work of the U.S. federal government and therefore in the public domain. Nurses’ sleep: Witkoski Stimpfel et al., NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing. The three portraits are written for this course to illustrate the data.

A full-time worker works 8.4 hours on a weekday and 5.6 hours at the weekend. Eighty per cent of employed people work on a weekday, but only thirty per cent work at the weekend. They sleep about nine hours and spend nearly five on leisure, half of it television.

That is the average. Here are three people nowhere near it.

Aliya is a night nurse. Her shift runs from seven in the evening to seven in the morning. She hardly ever eats a proper meal at work, and she rarely sleeps well: nurses sleep about eighty-three minutes less before a shift. On her days off she stays in, does the housework, helps her son with his homework and goes swimming twice a week.

Dias is a freelancer. A third of employed people now work from home; Dias does it every day. He writes a to-do list each morning and works indoors until dark. He often works late. He never goes to the gym and gave up running years ago, but he plays chess online twice a week.

Ruslan is a farmer. He gets up early, always, even in winter, and spends the day outdoors. His work is his exercise. In summer he hardly ever has a free weekend, but every October he goes camping.

The survey gives you a number. It does not give you a day. Ask any of the three of them what a normal week looks like, and all three will tell you theirs is completely ordinary.

Sources. All national figures: American Time Use Survey 2024, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — a work of the U.S. federal government and therefore in the public domain. Nurses’ sleep: Witkoski Stimpfel et al., NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing. The three portraits are written for this course to illustrate the data.

steps.title: Whose week would you find hardest?
steps.html: Use a frequency adverb in every reason: I could never…, I hardly ever…, I usually…

steps.title: After reading
steps.html: Compare yourself with the survey, not with the three people. Do you sleep more or less than nine hours? Do you spend more or less than five hours on leisure? Write three sentences, each with a different frequency adverb.

steps.title: Write about your own typical week.

steps.html:
1. Plan: the morning → work or study → the evening → the weekend.

  • Something you usually do
  • Something you sometimes do
  • Something you never do
  • Something you do once or twice a week
  • Something you do every day
